Simhala, or Sinhala, is the old name of the island of Sri Lanka and of its main people, the Sinhalese. The map uses it for the island from 500 BCE to 700 CE, the age of the kingdom of Anuradhapura.

The Sinhalese speak Sinhala, an Indo-Aryan language. Their chronicle, the Mahavamsa, says they descend from Prince Vijaya, who sailed from north India around 543 BCE. Historians treat this as legend, but the language shows that settlers from north India did come, and mixed with people from South India and the island's earlier inhabitants.

The key moments of the period:

  • About 377 BCE, Anuradhapura became the capital. Its kings built huge reservoirs, called tanks, to water rice fields in the dry zone.
  • About 250 BCE, Mahinda, said to be the son of the Indian emperor Ashoka, brought Buddhism. King Devanampiya Tissa accepted it, and Sri Lanka became a centre of Theravada Buddhism, which it later passed to Burma and Thailand.
  • Around 100 BCE, the Pali Buddhist scriptures were first written down on the island.
  • Late 400s CE, King Kashyapa built the rock fortress of Sigiriya.

Through these centuries the island traded with Rome, Persia and China, and wars with Tamil kings of South India, such as the Cholas and Pandyas, recurred. Today the Sinhalese are about three-quarters of Sri Lanka's people.
sum: Simhala, or Sinhala, is the old name of the island of Sri Lanka and of its main people, the Sinhalese. The map uses it for the island from 500 BCE to 700 CE, the age of the kingdom of Anuradhapura.
